lesson.title: Differentiating in Motion: Implicit Differentiation with Respect to Time
lesson.summary: Related rates equations are differentiated implicitly with respect to time using the exact same chain rule and product rule machinery from implicit differentiation, just with every variable now understood to be a hidden function of t.
lesson.body:
When you first learned implicit differentiation, the setup was an equation like x^2 + y^2 = 25, and the trick was to treat y as an unspecified function of x, so that differentiating y^2 with respect to x required the chain rule and produced 2y (dy/dx). Related rates asks you to take one more conceptual step: now both x and y are treated as functions of a third variable, time t, and you differentiate the whole equation with respect to t instead of x. The rules are identical, only the variable you are differentiating with respect to has changed.

That means every term in the equation now needs its own dt factor, tracked carefully. A power like x^n differentiates to n x^(n-1) (dx/dt), by the power rule combined with the chain rule. A product like xy, where both factors are changing, differentiates to x (dy/dt) + y (dx/dt), by the ordinary product rule, except now both derivative factors are with respect to t rather than being the implicit 1 you get from dx/dx. A trig term like sin x differentiates to cos x (dx/dt). The one thing to watch closely is that nothing gets treated as a plain constant just because it looks like a fixed variable name: if a quantity is changing over time, its derivative term has to appear.

Here is a worked example to make the mechanics concrete. Suppose x^2 + y^2 = 25 and, at the point (3, 4), dx/dt = 2. Find dy/dt at that instant. First check that the point actually satisfies the equation: 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so it does. Differentiate both sides with respect to t: 2x (dx/dt) + 2y (dy/dt) = 0, since the right side is a constant. Divide through by 2: x (dx/dt) + y (dy/dt) = 0. Now substitute the known values, x = 3, y = 4, dx/dt = 2: 3(2) + 4 (dy/dt) = 0, so 6 + 4 (dy/dt) = 0, giving dy/dt = -1.5. The negative sign is meaningful: at this instant, y is decreasing at 1.5 units for every unit of time, even though x is increasing.

This is precisely the tool that related rates relies on. A geometric constraint, a circle equation, a Pythagorean relationship, a similar triangles ratio, is really a family of equations, one for each moment in time, and differentiating it with respect to t in context reveals exactly how the rates of the individual variables are locked together. Everything from here forward, sorting rates from static values, drawing the diagram, and working the five classic problem types, is an application of this same implicit differentiation in context, over and over, in different geometric settings.
